topic: A. Introduction to Medicine and Medical Science (IMMS)
case_context: A 30-year-old couple attends a preconception genetic counselling session. They are concerned because both of their families have a history of a common autosomal recessive condition. The counsellor explains the molecular basis of inheritance, starting with the structure of DNA.
question: In the normal double-helix structure of DNA, name the two purine bases and identify their respective pyrimidine pairing partners.
acceptable_answers: Adenine and Guanine; Adenine pairs with Thymine, Guanine pairs with Cytosine
Purines: Adenine (A) and Guanine (G); Pairs: A-T and G-C
Adenine pairs with Thymine; Guanine pairs with Cytosine
feedback: [Subtopic: Genetics] In DNA, the purines are Adenine and Guanine. According to Chargaff's rules for base pairing, Adenine (purine) always pairs with Thymine (pyrimidine) via two hydrogen bonds, and Guanine (purine) always pairs with Cytosine (pyrimidine) via three hydrogen bonds.

topic: A. Introduction to Medicine and Medical Science (IMMS)
case_context: A 30-year-old couple attends a preconception genetic counselling session. They are concerned because both of their families have a history of a common autosomal recessive condition. The counsellor explains the molecular basis of inheritance, starting with the structure of DNA.
additional_context: Genetic testing confirms that both the husband and wife are heterozygous carriers for the same autosomal recessive mutation.
question: State the percentage probability that their first child will be a carrier of the condition, and the percentage probability that the child will be homozygous dominant (wild-type) for the gene.
feedback: [Subtopic: Genetics] In an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern with two carrier parents (Aa x Aa), the offspring probabilities are: 25% homozygous dominant (AA), 50% heterozygous carriers (Aa), and 25% homozygous recessive/affected (aa).

topic: A. Introduction to Medicine and Medical Science (IMMS)
case_context: A 30-year-old couple attends a preconception genetic counselling session. They are concerned because both of their families have a history of a common autosomal recessive condition. The counsellor explains the molecular basis of inheritance, starting with the structure of DNA.
additional_context: The counsellor discusses the ΔF508 mutation, which is the most common variant associated with the condition in their population. This mutation affects the processing of a chloride channel protein.
question: Identify the specific category of DNA mutation (e.g., substitution, deletion, insertion) that characterizes the ΔF508 variant and name the specific amino acid that is missing from the resulting polypeptide chain.
feedback: [Subtopic: ILA 1 - Cystic Fibrosis] The ΔF508 mutation is a deletion of three nucleotides (CTT or AAA) which results in the loss of a single amino acid, Phenylalanine (F), at position 508 of the CFTR protein.

topic: A. Introduction to Medicine and Medical Science (IMMS)
case_context: A 30-year-old couple attends a preconception genetic counselling session. They are concerned because both of their families have a history of a common autosomal recessive condition. The counsellor explains the molecular basis of inheritance, starting with the structure of DNA.
additional_context: The CFTR protein must fold into a specific three-dimensional shape to function correctly as a transmembrane channel.
question: Name the specific covalent bond that links amino acids together to form the primary structure of a protein, and name the two most common structural motifs found in the secondary structure of proteins.
acceptable_answers: Peptide bond; Alpha helix and Beta-pleated sheet
Peptide; alpha helices and beta sheets
feedback: [Subtopic: Energy metabolism / Biochemistry] Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds (covalent) in the primary structure. The secondary structure is characterized by local folding patterns, primarily the alpha helix and the beta-pleated sheet, stabilized by hydrogen bonding.

topic: A. Introduction to Medicine and Medical Science (IMMS)
case_context: A 30-year-old couple attends a preconception genetic counselling session. They are concerned because both of their families have a history of a common autosomal recessive condition. The counsellor explains the molecular basis of inheritance, starting with the structure of DNA.
additional_context: Once successfully folded, the chloride channel protein is embedded into the plasma membrane to regulate ion movement.
question: Name the primary class of lipid that forms the structural bilayer of the cell membrane and state the descriptive term for a molecule that contains both a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail.
feedback: [Subtopic: Cell biology] The plasma membrane is primarily composed of a phospholipid bilayer. Molecules like phospholipids, which possess both a polar (hydrophilic) head and a non-polar (hydrophobic) tail, are described as amphipathic.

subtopic: Anatomical features of the cardiovascular system
case_context: A 25-year-old male athlete attends a sports physiology laboratory for a baseline assessment. As part of the assessment, a standard posteroanterior (PA) chest X-ray is reviewed to confirm normal heart size and position.
question: Name the cardiac chamber that forms the right border of the heart on a PA chest X-ray and the major venous vessel that enters its superior aspect.
acceptable_answers: Right atrium and Superior vena cava
feedback: [Subtopic: Anatomical features of the cardiovascular system] On a normal PA chest radiograph, the right border of the heart is formed by the right atrium. The superior vena cava enters the right atrium from above, carrying deoxygenated blood from the upper body.

subtopic: Physiological features of the cardiovascular system
case_context: A 25-year-old male athlete attends a sports physiology laboratory for a baseline assessment. As part of the assessment, a standard posteroanterior (PA) chest X-ray is reviewed to confirm normal heart size and position.
additional_context: During the physical examination, the athlete's resting blood pressure is measured at 120/75 mmHg.
question: Calculate this patient's mean arterial pressure (MAP) using the formula involving systolic and diastolic pressures. Include the correct units in your answer.
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the cardiovascular system] MAP is calculated as Diastolic Blood Pressure + 1/3(Pulse Pressure). Here: 75 + 1/3(120-75) = 75 + 15 = 90 mmHg.

case_context: A 25-year-old male athlete attends a sports physiology laboratory for a baseline assessment. As part of the assessment, a standard posteroanterior (PA) chest X-ray is reviewed to confirm normal heart size and position.
additional_context: The assessment includes a discussion on the efficiency of his cardiac muscle in comparison to skeletal muscle.
question: Cardiac myocytes are linked by specialized junctions called intercalated discs. Name the specific cell junction type within these discs that provides low-resistance electrical coupling between cells.
feedback: [Subtopic: Histology of the cardiovascular system] Intercalated discs contain desmosomes (for mechanical adhesion) and gap junctions. Gap junctions allow the rapid spread of action potentials between myocytes, enabling the heart to function as a functional syncytium.

subtopic: Physiological features of the cardiovascular system
case_context: A 25-year-old male athlete attends a sports physiology laboratory for a baseline assessment. As part of the assessment, a standard posteroanterior (PA) chest X-ray is reviewed to confirm normal heart size and position.
additional_context: A 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is performed, showing a normal sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 60 beats per minute.
question: State the specific physiological event occurring in the heart that is represented by the QRS complex on the ECG.
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the cardiovascular system] The QRS complex represents the rapid depolarisation of the right and left ventricles. This electrical event precedes ventricular contraction (systole).

case_context: A 25-year-old male athlete attends a sports physiology laboratory for a baseline assessment. As part of the assessment, a standard posteroanterior (PA) chest X-ray is reviewed to confirm normal heart size and position.
additional_context: A full blood count is taken as part of the health screen.
question: Name the most abundant type of leucocyte (white blood cell) found in a normal adult blood film, which typically possesses a multi-lobed nucleus.
feedback: [Subtopic: Principle features of haematology] Neutrophils are the most numerous leucocytes in the blood (typically 40-75%). They are granulocytes characterized by a multi-lobed nucleus (usually 3-5 lobes).

subtopic: Embryonic development of the heart and circulation
case_context: A 25-year-old male athlete attends a sports physiology laboratory for a baseline assessment. As part of the assessment, a standard posteroanterior (PA) chest X-ray is reviewed to confirm normal heart size and position.
additional_context: The athlete asks about how the heart develops before birth.
question: Name the physiological opening in the fetal interatrial septum that allows blood to bypass the non-functional lungs, and name the shallow depression that persists in the adult heart after this opening closes.
feedback: [Subtopic: Embryonic development of the heart and circulation] The foramen ovale is a fetal shunt allowing blood to flow from the right atrium to the left atrium. After birth, it closes to become the fossa ovalis.

subtopic: Anatomical features of the respiratory system / thorax
case_context: A 22-year-old medical student participates in a respiratory physiology workshop. They are hooked up to a spirometer and then perform a series of exercise tests to observe changes in ventilation and lung function.
question: Name the primary muscle of inspiration and state the specific spinal cord segments that provide its motor innervation via the phrenic nerve.
feedback: [Subtopic: Anatomical features of the respiratory system / thorax] The diaphragm is the most important muscle of inspiration. It is innervated by the phrenic nerves, which arise from the ventral rami of the C3, C4, and C5 spinal nerves ('C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive').

subtopic: Physiological features of the respiratory system
case_context: A 22-year-old medical student participates in a respiratory physiology workshop. They are hooked up to a spirometer and then perform a series of exercise tests to observe changes in ventilation and lung function.
additional_context: During the workshop, the student performs spirometry to measure various lung volumes and capacities. One capacity of interest is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal, quiet expiration.
question: Identify the two specific static lung volumes that, when summed together, constitute the Functional Residual Capacity (FRC).
acceptable_answers: Expiratory Reserve Volume and Residual Volume
Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) and Residual Volume (RV)
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the respiratory system] Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs at the end of a passive expiration. It is the sum of the Expiratory Reserve Volume (the extra air that can be expired) and the Residual Volume (the air that cannot be expired).

subtopic: Physiological features of the respiratory system
case_context: A 22-year-old medical student participates in a respiratory physiology workshop. They are hooked up to a spirometer and then perform a series of exercise tests to observe changes in ventilation and lung function.
additional_context: The student then performs an exercise test on a treadmill, causing their ventilation rate to increase in response to metabolic demands.
question: Name the two anatomical locations where peripheral chemoreceptors are found that monitor changes in arterial blood gases and pH.
acceptable_answers: The bifurcation of the common carotid arteries and the aortic arch
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the respiratory system] Peripheral chemoreceptors are located in the carotid bodies (at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries) and the aortic bodies (in the aortic arch). They primarily detect decreases in PaO2 and increases in PaCO2 and H+ concentration.

case_context: A 22-year-old medical student participates in a respiratory physiology workshop. They are hooked up to a spirometer and then perform a series of exercise tests to observe changes in ventilation and lung function.
additional_context: To reinforce their understanding of the gas exchange surface, the instructor shows the student a high-magnification micrograph of the alveoli.
question: Identify the squamous cell type that forms 95% of the alveolar surface area and name the cuboidal cell type responsible for producing pulmonary surfactant.
acceptable_answers: Type I pneumocyte and Type II pneumocyte
Type 1 alveolar cell and Type 2 alveolar cell
Type I pneumocytes and Type II pneumocytes
feedback: [Subtopic: Histology of the respiratory system] Type I pneumocytes are extremely thin squamous cells optimized for gas exchange, covering the vast majority of the alveolar surface. Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal cells that secrete pulmonary surfactant and act as progenitor cells for Type I cells.

subtopic: Physiological features of the respiratory system
case_context: A 22-year-old medical student participates in a respiratory physiology workshop. They are hooked up to a spirometer and then perform a series of exercise tests to observe changes in ventilation and lung function.
additional_context: The student asks why the smallest alveoli in the lungs do not simply collapse into the larger ones during expiration.
question: State the physical law that relates the collapsing pressure of an alveolus to its surface tension and radius, and identify the primary phospholipid component of surfactant that prevents this collapse.
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the respiratory system] Laplace's Law (P=2T/r) states that collapsing pressure (P) is proportional to surface tension (T) and inversely proportional to radius (r). Surfactant, primarily composed of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC), reduces surface tension more effectively in smaller alveoli, preventing collapse.

subtopic: Anatomical features of the gastrointestinal tract and liver, and abdomen
case_context: A 24-year-old man presents with dull, poorly localized pain in the epigastric region of his abdomen.
question: Name the major sympathetic nerve plexus through which visceral afferent fibers from the stomach and proximal duodenum pass to reach the spinal cord, leading to referred pain in this region.
feedback: [Subtopic: Anatomical features of the gastrointestinal tract and liver, and abdomen] Visceral afferent fibers from the foregut follow the sympathetic pathways (via the greater splanchnic nerves) back to the celiac plexus and then to the T5-T9 spinal segments. Because these segments also receive somatic input from the epigastric skin, the pain is referred to that region.

case_context: A 24-year-old man presents with dull, poorly localized pain in the epigastric region of his abdomen.
additional_context: The patient's stomach is functioning normally to produce digestive secretions.
question: Identify the specific cell type located within the gastric glands that is responsible for the secretion of hydrochloric acid (HCl) and intrinsic factor.
feedback: [Subtopic: ILA 5 - Gastritis and Appendicitis] Parietal cells (also known as oxyntic cells) are found in the gastric pits/glands of the fundus and body of the stomach. They produce HCl to lower the pH of the stomach and intrinsic factor for Vitamin B12 absorption.

subtopic: Anatomical features of the gastrointestinal tract and liver, and abdomen
case_context: A 24-year-old man presents with dull, poorly localized pain in the epigastric region of his abdomen.
additional_context: Proper blood supply is essential for the maintenance of the gastric mucosal barrier.
question: Name the main arterial trunk, which branches directly from the abdominal aorta at the level of T12, that provides the primary blood supply to the stomach and other foregut structures.
feedback: [Subtopic: Anatomical features of the gastrointestinal tract and liver, and abdomen] The celiac trunk is the first major branch of the abdominal aorta. It divides into the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries to supply the foregut.

subtopic: Histology of the gastrointestinal tract and liver
case_context: A 24-year-old man presents with dull, poorly localized pain in the epigastric region of his abdomen.
additional_context: The stomach has unique histological features to facilitate the mechanical churning of food.
question: State the specific muscular layer of the muscularis externa that is unique to the stomach compared to the rest of the gastrointestinal tract.
feedback: [Subtopic: Histology of the gastrointestinal tract and liver] Unlike the rest of the GI tract which typically has two layers of smooth muscle (inner circular and outer longitudinal), the stomach has a third, innermost layer called the oblique layer to assist in mechanical digestion.

subtopic: Embryonic development of the gastrointestinal tract and liver
case_context: A 24-year-old man presents with dull, poorly localized pain in the epigastric region of his abdomen.
additional_context: The final position of the stomach is determined by specific movements during embryogenesis.
question: State the degree (in degrees) and the direction of rotation the stomach undergoes around its longitudinal axis during embryonic development.
feedback: [Subtopic: Embryonic development of the gastrointestinal tract and liver] During development, the stomach rotates 90 degrees clockwise around its longitudinal axis. This results in the left vagus nerve becoming the anterior vagal trunk and the right vagus nerve becoming the posterior vagal trunk.

case_context: A 28-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department following a high-impact road traffic collision. He has sustained a vertebral fracture. Neurological examination reveals a loss of pain and temperature sensation on his right side below the level of the umbilicus, while proprioception and vibration sense are preserved on that side.
question: Name the specific ascending spinal tract that transmits pain and temperature information to the brain.
feedback: [Subtopic: Neuroanatomy] The lateral spinothalamic tract is responsible for the transmission of pain (nociception) and temperature information from the periphery to the thalamus.

case_context: A 28-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department following a high-impact road traffic collision. He has sustained a vertebral fracture. Neurological examination reveals a loss of pain and temperature sensation on his right side below the level of the umbilicus, while proprioception and vibration sense are preserved on that side.
additional_context: Sensory information from the skin is organized into dermatomes corresponding to specific spinal cord segments.
question: Identify the spinal cord segment that corresponds to the dermatome at the level of the umbilicus.
feedback: [Subtopic: Neuroanatomy] The T10 spinal segment provides the sensory innervation for the skin surrounding the umbilicus.

case_context: A 28-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department following a high-impact road traffic collision. He has sustained a vertebral fracture. Neurological examination reveals a loss of pain and temperature sensation on his right side below the level of the umbilicus, while proprioception and vibration sense are preserved on that side.
additional_context: To perceive a stimulus, an action potential must be generated and propagated along the primary afferent neuron.
question: During the depolarisation phase of an action potential, which specific ion channel opens to allow a rapid influx of ions into the axon?
feedback: [Subtopic: Neurophysiology] Depolarisation is driven by the opening of voltage-gated sodium channels, allowing Na+ to enter the cell down its electrochemical gradient.

case_context: A 28-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department following a high-impact road traffic collision. He has sustained a vertebral fracture. Neurological examination reveals a loss of pain and temperature sensation on his right side below the level of the umbilicus, while proprioception and vibration sense are preserved on that side.
additional_context: The primary afferent neuron in the pain pathway synapses with a second-order neuron within the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.
question: Name the primary excitatory neurotransmitter released by the first-order neuron at this synapse in the pain pathway.
feedback: [Subtopic: Neurophysiology] Glutamate is the primary fast excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS, while Substance P is a neuropeptide involved in the transmission of pain signals.

case_context: A 28-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department following a high-impact road traffic collision. He has sustained a vertebral fracture. Neurological examination reveals a loss of pain and temperature sensation on his right side below the level of the umbilicus, while proprioception and vibration sense are preserved on that side.
additional_context: The injury occurred at the level of the thoracic vertebrae.
question: State one anatomical feature of a typical thoracic vertebra that distinguishes it from cervical or lumbar vertebrae.
feedback: [Subtopic: Neuroanatomy] Thoracic vertebrae are unique because they possess costal facets (on the bodies and transverse processes) for articulation with the ribs.

case_context: A 28-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department following a high-impact road traffic collision. He has sustained a vertebral fracture. Neurological examination reveals a loss of pain and temperature sensation on his right side below the level of the umbilicus, while proprioception and vibration sense are preserved on that side.
additional_context: Pain perception involves different types of nerve fibres that conduct signals at different speeds.
question: Identify the specific type of unmyelinated nerve fibre responsible for transmitting slow, dull, aching pain.
feedback: [Subtopic: Neurophysiology] C fibres are small-diameter, unmyelinated fibres that conduct signals slowly (0.5–2.0 m/s) and are associated with 'second' or dull, aching pain.

topic: F. Skin, UroGenital, Endocrine and Reproduction (SUGER)
subtopic: Physiological features of the reproductive system
case_context: A 28-year-old woman presents to her GP for preconception counseling. She has a regular 28-day menstrual cycle and is tracking her ovulation in hopes of conceiving.
question: Name the hypothalamic hormone that is released in a pulsatile manner to stimulate the anterior pituitary gland to secrete follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH).
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the reproductive system] The HPO axis begins with the pulsatile release of GnRH from the hypothalamus, which acts on the gonadotrophs of the anterior pituitary.

topic: F. Skin, UroGenital, Endocrine and Reproduction (SUGER)
subtopic: Physiological features of the reproductive system
case_context: A 28-year-old woman presents to her GP for preconception counseling. She has a regular 28-day menstrual cycle and is tracking her ovulation in hopes of conceiving.
additional_context: During the follicular phase, the recruitment and maturation of follicles involves complex hormonal interactions between the pituitary and the ovary, often referred to as the 'two-cell, two-gonadotropin' theory.
question: Identify the specific layer of cells within the ovarian follicle that is stimulated by LH to produce androgens (such as androstenedione).
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the reproductive system] According to the two-cell theory, LH stimulates theca cells to produce androgens, which then diffuse to the granulosa cells to be converted into oestrogen via aromatase (stimulated by FSH).

topic: F. Skin, UroGenital, Endocrine and Reproduction (SUGER)
subtopic: Physiological features of the endocrine system
case_context: A 28-year-old woman presents to her GP for preconception counseling. She has a regular 28-day menstrual cycle and is tracking her ovulation in hopes of conceiving.
additional_context: Successful ovulation requires a switch from negative to positive feedback by oestrogen on the pituitary gland and hypothalamus.
question: Name the pituitary hormone that reaches a peak concentration ('surge') approximately 24 to 36 hours before ovulation occurs.
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the endocrine system] High levels of oestrogen at the end of the follicular phase trigger a positive feedback loop, resulting in a surge of LH from the anterior pituitary, which triggers the final maturation and release of the oocyte.

topic: F. Skin, UroGenital, Endocrine and Reproduction (SUGER)
case_context: A 28-year-old woman presents to her GP for preconception counseling. She has a regular 28-day menstrual cycle and is tracking her ovulation in hopes of conceiving.
additional_context: Following ovulation, the lining of the uterus undergoes specific histological changes to prepare for potential implantation.
question: Name the specific histological layer of the endometrium that is shed during the menstrual phase of the cycle.
feedback: [Subtopic: Histology of SUGER] The endometrium is divided into the stratum basalis (which remains intact) and the stratum functionalis. The stratum functionalis proliferates and becomes secretory during the cycle but is shed if fertilisation does not occur.

topic: F. Skin, UroGenital, Endocrine and Reproduction (SUGER)
subtopic: Physiological features of the reproductive system
case_context: A 28-year-old woman presents to her GP for preconception counseling. She has a regular 28-day menstrual cycle and is tracking her ovulation in hopes of conceiving.
additional_context: The corpus luteum is formed from the remnants of the Graafian follicle and acts as a temporary endocrine organ during the luteal phase.
question: Name the steroid hormone produced in high quantities by the corpus luteum that induces the 'secretory phase' of the uterine cycle.
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the reproductive system] Progesterone is the dominant hormone of the luteal phase. It induces secretory changes in the endometrium (tortuous glands, increased vascularity) to facilitate implantation.

topic: F. Skin, UroGenital, Endocrine and Reproduction (SUGER)
subtopic: Anatomical features of the urogenital and pelvic organs
case_context: A 28-year-old woman presents to her GP for preconception counseling. She has a regular 28-day menstrual cycle and is tracking her ovulation in hopes of conceiving.
additional_context: If coitus occurs during the fertile window, sperm must travel from the vagina through the cervix and uterus to reach the site of fertilisation.
question: Identify the specific anatomical region of the uterine (fallopian) tube where fertilisation most commonly occurs.
feedback: [Subtopic: Anatomical features of the urogenital and pelvic organs] The ampulla is the widest and longest part of the uterine tube, situated between the infundibulum and the isthmus, and is the physiological site of fertilisation.

case_context: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after falling onto her outstretched right hand. She has an obvious "dinner-fork" deformity of the wrist. Radiographs confirm a fracture of the distal radius.
question: List the two carpal bones that articulate directly with the distal radius to form the radiocarpal joint.
feedback: [Subtopic: ILA 10 - Distal Radius Fracture] The distal radius articulates with the scaphoid and lunate bones of the proximal carpal row. The triquetrum articulates with the articular disc of the distal radioulnar joint, not the radius itself.

case_context: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after falling onto her outstretched right hand. She has an obvious "dinner-fork" deformity of the wrist. Radiographs confirm a fracture of the distal radius.
additional_context: The outer layer of the radius consists of dense, cortical bone organized into functional microscopic units.
question: Name the structural units that comprise cortical bone and the central canal within each unit that houses the neurovascular bundle.
feedback: [Subtopic: Histology] Cortical (compact) bone is made of repeating units called osteons (or Haversian systems). Each osteon contains a central Haversian canal containing blood vessels and nerves.

case_context: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after falling onto her outstretched right hand. She has an obvious "dinner-fork" deformity of the wrist. Radiographs confirm a fracture of the distal radius.
additional_context: The mechanical strength of the radius is provided by its specialized extracellular matrix.
question: Name the primary type of collagen found in the organic bone matrix and the specific calcium-phosphate mineral crystal that makes up the inorganic component.
feedback: [Subtopic: Bone] Bone matrix is a composite material. The organic part is primarily Type 1 collagen (providing tensile strength), while the inorganic part is hydroxyapatite (providing compressive strength).

case_context: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after falling onto her outstretched right hand. She has an obvious "dinner-fork" deformity of the wrist. Radiographs confirm a fracture of the distal radius.
additional_context: Mineral homeostasis is essential for normal bone maintenance and the healing process following a fracture.
question: Name the hormone secreted by the parathyroid glands in response to low serum calcium and identify the bone-resorbing cell type it indirectly stimulates to release calcium into the blood.
feedback: [Subtopic: Biochemistry/homeostasis] Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is released when blood calcium is low. It binds to receptors on osteoblasts, which then signal to osteoclasts (via RANKL) to increase bone resorption.

case_context: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after falling onto her outstretched right hand. She has an obvious "dinner-fork" deformity of the wrist. Radiographs confirm a fracture of the distal radius.
additional_context: The clinician assesses the patient's motor function to ensure the injury has not compromised the nerves supplying the forearm muscles.
question: Name the neurotransmitter released at the neuromuscular junction to initiate skeletal muscle contraction and the specific ion whose influx into the nerve terminal triggers this release.
feedback: [Subtopic: Muscle] At the neuromuscular junction, an action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal, opening voltage-gated calcium channels. The resulting calcium influx triggers the exocytosis of acetylcholine (ACh).

subtopic: Sustainable prescribing (linked to 'Asthma / Sustainable healthcare' - EYGP session 4)
case_context: A 62-year-old man presents to his GP for a review of his asthma and chronic knee pain caused by osteoarthritis. He is currently prescribed a salbutamol metered-dose inhaler (MDI) and an oral strong opiate.
question: Name the specific class of greenhouse gases used as propellants in Metered Dose Inhalers (MDIs) that contribute to their high carbon footprint, and state the alternative type of inhaler device that does not require these propellants.
acceptable_answers: Fluorinated gases and Dry Powder Inhaler
feedback: [Subtopic: Sustainable prescribing (linked to 'Asthma / Sustainable healthcare' - EYGP session 4)] MDIs use hydrofluoroalkanes (HFAs) as propellants, which are potent greenhouse gases. Dry Powder Inhalers (DPIs) do not use propellants and generally have a much lower environmental impact.

subtopic: Drugs associated with dependence and withdrawal symptoms (linked to 'Osteoarthritis / Chronic pain - EYGP session 11)
case_context: A 62-year-old man presents to his GP for a review of his asthma and chronic knee pain caused by osteoarthritis. He is currently prescribed a salbutamol metered-dose inhaler (MDI) and an oral strong opiate.
additional_context: The patient reports that his opiate medication is no longer as effective at relieving his pain as it was six months ago.
question: State the physiological term used to describe the requirement for increasing doses of a drug to achieve the same effect, and name the cellular process involving receptors that typically underlies this phenomenon.
feedback: [Subtopic: Drugs associated with dependence and withdrawal symptoms (linked to 'Osteoarthritis / Chronic pain - EYGP session 11)] Tolerance occurs when the body's response to a drug decreases over time, often due to the downregulation or internalisation of receptors in response to chronic stimulation.

subtopic: Use of FP10 prescriptions in Primary Care (linked to 'Generalism and holistic patient care' - EYGP session 1)
case_context: A 62-year-old man presents to his GP for a review of his asthma and chronic knee pain caused by osteoarthritis. He is currently prescribed a salbutamol metered-dose inhaler (MDI) and an oral strong opiate.
additional_context: The GP decides to issue a new FP10 prescription for the patient's medications.
question: According to UK legal requirements for a valid prescription, name TWO patient-specific identifiers that must be present on the FP10 form.
feedback: [Subtopic: Use of FP10 prescriptions in Primary Care (linked to 'Generalism and holistic patient care' - EYGP session 1)] For a prescription to be legally valid for dispensing, it must include the patient's name, the patient's address, the prescriber's name/address/signature, the date, and the particulars of the drug (name, dose, strength, quantity).

subtopic: Routes of drug administration and medicine formulations (linked to 'Ischaemic heart disease / Health inequalities' - EYGP session 3)
case_context: A 62-year-old man presents to his GP for a review of his asthma and chronic knee pain caused by osteoarthritis. He is currently prescribed a salbutamol metered-dose inhaler (MDI) and an oral strong opiate.
question: Classify the salbutamol inhaler's route of administration in terms of its intended site of action (local or systemic), and name the specific level of the lower respiratory tract it primarily targets to produce bronchodilation.
feedback: [Subtopic: Routes of drug administration and medicine formulations (linked to 'Ischaemic heart disease / Health inequalities' - EYGP session 3)] Inhaled medications for asthma are intended for local administration to act directly on the smooth muscle of the bronchi and bronchioles.

subtopic: Adherence and non-adherence (linked to 'Chronic kidney disease (CKD) / Accessing healthcare for non-English speaking populations' - EYGP session 9)
case_context: A 62-year-old man presents to his GP for a review of his asthma and chronic knee pain caused by osteoarthritis. He is currently prescribed a salbutamol metered-dose inhaler (MDI) and an oral strong opiate.
additional_context: During the consultation, the patient mentions that he frequently forgets to take his evening doses of medication because he gets distracted by the television.
question: Classify this specific type of non-adherence and state one practical strategy (other than education) that could be used to help the patient remember his doses.
acceptable_answers: Unintentional non-adherence and Multi-compartment compliance aids
Unintentional non-adherence and Linking to daily routine
feedback: [Subtopic: Adherence and non-adherence (linked to 'Chronic kidney disease (CKD) / Accessing healthcare for non-English speaking populations' - EYGP session 9)] Unintentional non-adherence occurs when a patient wants to follow the treatment plan but is prevented by barriers like forgetfulness. Strategies include reminders (alarms), multi-compartment compliance aids (dosette boxes), or habit-stacking (linking medication to a routine like brushing teeth).

case_context: A local GP practice in an urban area is reviewing their population health data. They observe that the community has high rates of respiratory illness, poor housing quality, and low uptake of seasonal vaccinations.
additional_context: To address these issues, the practice works with the regional Public Health England (or equivalent) team, which operates across three main pillars of public health.
question: Name the specific pillar of public health that focuses on protecting the population from infectious diseases, chemicals, and environmental hazards, such as the management of a local tuberculosis outbreak.
feedback: [Subtopic: Three pillars of public health] The three pillars of public health are health protection, health improvement, and health services. Health protection involves responding to infectious diseases and environmental hazards.

case_context: A local GP practice in an urban area is reviewing their population health data. They observe that the community has high rates of respiratory illness, poor housing quality, and low uptake of seasonal vaccinations.
question: What is the term used to describe the systematic, avoidable, and unfair differences in health status and outcomes between different groups of people, often driven by the conditions in which they are born and live?
feedback: [Subtopic: Address social determinants of health] Health inequities are unfair and avoidable differences in health across the population, and between different groups within society, arising from the social determinants of health.

case_context: A local GP practice in an urban area is reviewing their population health data. They observe that the community has high rates of respiratory illness, poor housing quality, and low uptake of seasonal vaccinations.
additional_context: A 45-year-old patient from this community is diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The patient expects to be excused from their job in a factory and expects their family to take over household chores.
question: According to the sociological theory developed by Talcott Parsons, what is the term for the set of social expectations and obligations that define the behavior of a person who is ill?
feedback: [Subtopic: Medical sociology] The 'Sick Role' is a concept in medical sociology that describes the rights (e.g., exemption from normal social roles) and obligations (e.g., seeking professional help and wanting to get well) of an ill person.

subtopic: Public health in practice – application of the principles of public health
case_context: A local GP practice in an urban area is reviewing their population health data. They observe that the community has high rates of respiratory illness, poor housing quality, and low uptake of seasonal vaccinations.
additional_context: The practice is considering implementing a new screening program for early detection of Type 2 Diabetes within their local population.
question: According to the Wilson and Jungner criteria for screening, what must be available for patients who are identified as having the condition through a screening test?
feedback: [Subtopic: Public health in practice – application of the principles of public health] One of the key Wilson and Jungner criteria is that there should be an accepted treatment for patients with recognized disease.

case_context: A local GP practice in an urban area is reviewing their population health data. They observe that the community has high rates of respiratory illness, poor housing quality, and low uptake of seasonal vaccinations.
additional_context: The GP wants to reduce the overall risk of cardiovascular disease in the entire community by encouraging all local shops to reduce the salt content in their pre-packaged meals, rather than only advising high-risk individuals to change their diet.
question: Name the prevention strategy, described by Geoffrey Rose, which aims to shift the distribution of a risk factor in the whole population rather than targeting only those at high risk.
feedback: [Subtopic: Behaviour and society] Rose's population strategy focuses on the whole population, aiming to reduce the level of risk for everyone, which can result in a large total benefit even if the benefit to each individual is small.

case_context: A group of researchers conducts a study to investigate whether a new 12-week daily stretching programme improves the range of motion (measured in degrees) in the hip joint of healthy adults. They recruit 200 participants from a local fitness centre.
additional_context: Participants are randomly allocated into two groups: one group performs the daily stretching programme, and the other group continues their usual activity level.
question: Name the specific type of quantitative study design described in this scenario.
feedback: [Subtopic: Quantitative study design] A study where participants are randomly assigned to an intervention or a control group to compare outcomes is a randomised controlled trial, which sits high on the hierarchy of evidence for intervention efficacy.

case_context: A group of researchers conducts a study to investigate whether a new 12-week daily stretching programme improves the range of motion (measured in degrees) in the hip joint of healthy adults. They recruit 200 participants from a local fitness centre.
additional_context: The primary outcome measure is the change in hip flexion range of motion, recorded in degrees (e.g., 120.5 degrees).
question: State the specific type of numerical data that 'degrees of motion' represents.
feedback: [Subtopic: Summary statistics] Numerical data that can take any value within a range and can be measured to decimal places (like degrees, height, or weight) is classified as continuous data.

case_context: A group of researchers conducts a study to investigate whether a new 12-week daily stretching programme improves the range of motion (measured in degrees) in the hip joint of healthy adults. They recruit 200 participants from a local fitness centre.
additional_context: The researchers set out to test the assumption that there is no difference in the mean range of motion between the stretching group and the control group.
question: Give the formal statistical term for the hypothesis that assumes no difference or effect exists between the two study groups.
feedback: [Subtopic: Inferential statistics] The null hypothesis (H0) is the starting assumption in hypothesis testing that there is no relationship between variables or no difference between groups.

case_context: A group of researchers conducts a study to investigate whether a new 12-week daily stretching programme improves the range of motion (measured in degrees) in the hip joint of healthy adults. They recruit 200 participants from a local fitness centre.
additional_context: The results show a mean improvement of 5 degrees in the stretching group compared to the control group. The 95% confidence interval for this difference is -1.5 to +11.5 degrees.
question: Based on the provided 95% confidence interval, state whether the result is statistically significant at the 5% level.
feedback: [Subtopic: Inferential statistics] When a 95% confidence interval for a difference between means includes the value of zero (null value), the result is not considered statistically significant at the p < 0.05 level.

case_context: A group of researchers conducts a study to investigate whether a new 12-week daily stretching programme improves the range of motion (measured in degrees) in the hip joint of healthy adults. They recruit 200 participants from a local fitness centre.
additional_context: It is noted that participants in the stretching group were significantly younger on average than those in the control group. Age is known to independently influence joint flexibility.
question: What is the specific statistical term for a variable, such as age in this study, that is associated with both the intervention and the outcome, potentially distorting the perceived relationship?
feedback: [Subtopic: Critical appraisal] A confounding variable is an extraneous factor that correlates with both the independent and dependent variables, leading to a possible false association if not controlled for.

feedback: [Subtopic: ○ Additional tests offered to screen for and diagnose foetal genetic abnormalities.] Routine screening includes the combined test (ultrasound and bloods) or the quadruple test. Diagnostic options include amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling (CVS).

case_context: A 32-year-old woman, Sarah, attends her first 'booking' appointment with her midwife at 10 weeks gestation. She has a past medical history of Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) and a family history of early-onset ischaemic heart disease.

question: List two specific dietary or nutritional supplement recommendations routinely given to pregnant women in the UK to promote fetal health or reduce the risk of birth defects.
acceptable_answers: Avoid unpasteurised dairy or soft cheeses
feedback: [Subtopic: Session 2 'Pregnancy' (during IMMS block)] Routine advice includes taking 400mcg of folic acid (to prevent neural tube defects) and 10mcg of vitamin D. Women are also advised to avoid foods high in Listeria (unpasteurised cheese) or high in Vitamin A (liver/pate).

subtopic: Session 5 'Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) / Functional disorders' (during GI-Liver block)
case_context: A 32-year-old woman, Sarah, attends her first 'booking' appointment with her midwife at 10 weeks gestation. She has a past medical history of Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) and a family history of early-onset ischaemic heart disease.

question: Briefly define the term 'functional illness' using non-medical language, as you would to a patient.
acceptable_answers: A condition where the body's processes (or how it works) are not functioning correctly, despite the structure appearing normal on tests or scans.
A condition where there is a problem with the way the body works rather than a physical or structural abnormality.
The body's 'software' is having an issue, even though the 'hardware' (organs) looks fine.
feedback: [Subtopic: Session 5 'Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) / Functional disorders' (during GI-Liver block)] A functional illness (like IBS) is defined by a disturbance in the function of an organ or system without any detectable structural change or physical abnormality on conventional medical investigation.

subtopic: Session 3 'Ischaemic heart disease / Health inequalities' (during Cardiovascular block)
case_context: A 32-year-old woman, Sarah, attends her first 'booking' appointment with her midwife at 10 weeks gestation. She has a past medical history of Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) and a family history of early-onset ischaemic heart disease.
additional_context: Discussing her family history of heart disease, the midwife mentions the importance of 'primary prevention' and 'secondary prevention'.
question: Define the difference between primary prevention and secondary prevention in the context of cardiovascular disease.
acceptable_answers: Primary prevention involves preventing the onset of disease in healthy individuals; secondary prevention involves preventing recurrence or progression in those who already have the disease.
Primary is for people without the disease; secondary is for people with the disease.
feedback: [Subtopic: Session 3 'Ischaemic heart disease / Health inequalities' (during Cardiovascular block)] Primary prevention aims to stop the disease from occurring in the first place (e.g., managing BP in healthy adults). Secondary prevention aims to reduce the impact of a disease that has already occurred (e.g., taking aspirin after a heart attack).

subtopic: Session 1 'Generalism and holistic patient care' (during IMMS block)
case_context: A 32-year-old woman, Sarah, attends her first 'booking' appointment with her midwife at 10 weeks gestation. She has a past medical history of Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) and a family history of early-onset ischaemic heart disease.

question: State two general differences between primary care and secondary care within the UK health system.
acceptable_answers: Primary care is the first point of contact whereas secondary care requires a referral.
Primary care is generalist whereas secondary care is specialist.
Primary care is community-based whereas secondary care is usually hospital-based.
feedback: [Subtopic: Session 1 'Generalism and holistic patient care' (during IMMS block)] Primary care (GPs, midwives, etc.) acts as the first point of contact and provides generalist care in the community. Secondary care provides specialist services and usually requires a referral from a primary care provider.

topic: A. Introduction to Medicine and Medical Science (IMMS)
case_context: A 24-year-old woman is attending a preconception genetic counseling session because her brother has Cystic Fibrosis. Her brother is known to be homozygous for the ΔF508 mutation.
question: The ΔF508 variant is the most common mutation in the CFTR gene. State the specific type of DNA mutation (e.g., substitution, insertion, or deletion) and the number of nucleotides involved that characterizes this variant.
feedback: [Subtopic: ILA 1 - Cystic Fibrosis] The ΔF508 mutation is a class II mutation involving the deletion of three nucleotides (CTT) which results in the loss of a single amino acid (phenylalanine) at position 508 of the CFTR protein.

topic: A. Introduction to Medicine and Medical Science (IMMS)
case_context: A 24-year-old woman is attending a preconception genetic counseling session because her brother has Cystic Fibrosis. Her brother is known to be homozygous for the ΔF508 mutation.
additional_context: The counselor explains that Cystic Fibrosis follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Both of the patient's parents are healthy.
question: Calculate the probability (expressed as a percentage or fraction) that the patient herself is a carrier of the CFTR mutation, given that she does not have the condition.
feedback: [Subtopic: Genetics] Since both parents must be carriers (Aa) for the brother to be affected (aa), the patient's possible genotypes are AA, Aa, or aA. Because she is healthy, the 'aa' possibility is excluded, leaving a 2 in 3 (66.7%) chance that she is a carrier.

topic: A. Introduction to Medicine and Medical Science (IMMS)
case_context: A 24-year-old woman is attending a preconception genetic counseling session because her brother has Cystic Fibrosis. Her brother is known to be homozygous for the ΔF508 mutation.
additional_context: The counselor describes how the normal CFTR protein functions within the plasma membrane of epithelial cells to transport chloride ions.
question: Name the specific type of membrane transport protein that uses the hydrolysis of ATP to move substances against a concentration gradient, of which the CFTR protein is a member.
feedback: [Subtopic: Cell biology] The CFTR protein belongs to the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter superfamily. Unlike most ABC transporters that act as pumps, CFTR functions as an ion channel, though it still binds and hydrolyses ATP to regulate its function.

topic: A. Introduction to Medicine and Medical Science (IMMS)

question: Name the specific type of covalent bond that links amino acids together in a protein's primary structure.
feedback: [Subtopic: Energy metabolism / Biochemistry] The primary structure of a protein is the linear sequence of amino acids held together by covalent peptide bonds, which form between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another.

case_context: A 24-year-old woman is attending a preconception genetic counseling session because her brother has Cystic Fibrosis. Her brother is known to be homozygous for the ΔF508 mutation.

question: Identify the specific type of epithelium (including any surface specialisations) that normally lines the majority of the conducting airways, such as the trachea and bronchi.
feedback: [Subtopic: Cell histology and their ultrastructural components] The respiratory tract is primarily lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, which contains goblet cells to produce mucus and cilia to move the mucus out of the airways (the mucociliary escalator).

subtopic: Anatomical features of the cardiovascular system
case_context: A 22-year-old student athlete attends a sports medicine clinic for a pre-participation screening. As part of the assessment, the physician performs a physical examination and reviews the surface anatomy of the heart in relation to the chest wall.
question: State the specific chamber of the heart that forms the majority of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart.
feedback: [Subtopic: Anatomical features of the cardiovascular system] The right ventricle occupies most of the anterior surface of the heart, while the left ventricle forms the apex and the left border.

subtopic: Physiological features of the cardiovascular system
case_context: A 22-year-old student athlete attends a sports medicine clinic for a pre-participation screening. As part of the assessment, the physician performs a physical examination and reviews the surface anatomy of the heart in relation to the chest wall.
additional_context: An electrocardiogram (ECG) is performed as part of the screening, which shows a normal sinus rhythm with a clearly defined P-wave.
question: Name the specific electrical event in the cardiac cycle that is represented by the P-wave on a normal ECG trace.
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the cardiovascular system] The P-wave represents the spread of electrical activity (depolarisation) from the SA node through the atrial musculature, preceding atrial contraction.

case_context: A 22-year-old student athlete attends a sports medicine clinic for a pre-participation screening. As part of the assessment, the physician performs a physical examination and reviews the surface anatomy of the heart in relation to the chest wall.
additional_context: The physician discusses the efficiency of the myocardium in coordinating contraction to maintain a high cardiac output during exercise.
question: Name the specialized intercellular junctions located within intercalated discs that provide low-resistance electrical coupling between adjacent cardiac myocytes.
feedback: [Subtopic: Histology of the cardiovascular system] Gap junctions allow for the rapid passage of ions between cells, ensuring the myocardium functions as a functional syncytium. They are found in the longitudinal portions of intercalated discs.

subtopic: Embryonic development of the heart and circulation
case_context: A 22-year-old student athlete attends a sports medicine clinic for a pre-participation screening. As part of the assessment, the physician performs a physical examination and reviews the surface anatomy of the heart in relation to the chest wall.
additional_context: During the screening, the athlete asks about how the heart changes at birth when the lungs begin to function.
question: Name the fetal vascular shunt that connects the pulmonary trunk directly to the descending aorta, normally closing shortly after birth to become the ligamentum arteriosum.
feedback: [Subtopic: Embryonic development of the heart and circulation] The ductus arteriosus allows blood to bypass the non-functional fetal lungs by shunting blood from the pulmonary artery to the systemic circulation.

case_context: A 22-year-old student athlete attends a sports medicine clinic for a pre-participation screening. As part of the assessment, the physician performs a physical examination and reviews the surface anatomy of the heart in relation to the chest wall.
additional_context: Routine blood tests are performed to ensure the athlete is healthy. The labs show a normal plasma protein profile.
question: Name the most abundant plasma protein that is primarily responsible for maintaining the colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure of the blood.
feedback: [Subtopic: Principle features of haematology] Albumin is the major plasma protein produced by the liver. It accounts for about 75-80% of the plasma colloid osmotic pressure, preventing excessive fluid loss from capillaries into the interstitial space.

subtopic: Physiological features of the respiratory system
case_context: A healthy 22-year-old male is participating in a baseline respiratory assessment for a sports science study. He is asked to perform several breathing manoeuvres while connected to a spirometer.
question: Name the lung volume that remains in the lungs following a maximal, forceful expiration and name the capacity that describes the maximum volume of air that can be exhaled following a maximal inhalation.
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the respiratory system] Residual volume (RV) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after maximal exhalation, which cannot be measured by simple spirometry. Vital capacity (VC) is the total volume of air that can be voluntarily moved in one breath (VC = IRV + TV + ERV).

subtopic: Anatomical features of the respiratory system / thorax
case_context: A healthy 22-year-old male is participating in a baseline respiratory assessment for a sports science study. He is asked to perform several breathing manoeuvres while connected to a spirometer.
additional_context: The assessment observes the movement of the primary muscle of inspiration during deep breathing.
question: Name the specific nerve that provides motor innervation to the diaphragm and state the spinal cord segments from which its fibres originate.
feedback: [Subtopic: Anatomical features of the respiratory system / thorax] The diaphragm is the primary muscle of respiration. It is innervated by the phrenic nerve, which arises from the ventral rami of the C3, C4, and C5 spinal nerves ('C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive').

case_context: A healthy 22-year-old male is participating in a baseline respiratory assessment for a sports science study. He is asked to perform several breathing manoeuvres while connected to a spirometer.
additional_context: The study includes a discussion on the efficiency of the blood-air barrier where gas exchange occurs at the microscopic level.
question: Name the specific type of alveolar epithelial cell that covers the majority of the alveolar surface area for gas exchange, and name the other cellular component that forms the blood-air barrier.
acceptable_answers: Type I pneumocyte and capillary endothelial cell
Type I alveolar cell and endothelial cell
feedback: [Subtopic: Histology of the respiratory system] The blood-air barrier is composed of the Type I pneumocyte (a thin squamous cell), the fused basement membrane, and the capillary endothelial cell. Type II pneumocytes are more numerous but cover less surface area as they produce surfactant.

subtopic: Anatomical features of the respiratory system / thorax
case_context: A healthy 22-year-old male is participating in a baseline respiratory assessment for a sports science study. He is asked to perform several breathing manoeuvres while connected to a spirometer.
additional_context: A physical examination of the thoracic cage is performed to identify surface landmarks used for auscultation.
question: Identify the anatomical landmark formed by the articulation of the manubrium and the body of the sternum, and state which rib articulates with the sternum at this specific level.
feedback: [Subtopic: Anatomical features of the respiratory system / thorax] The sternal angle (Angle of Louis) is a critical surface landmark at the T4/T5 vertebral level. It marks the site of the second costal cartilage/rib articulation, the bifurcation of the trachea, and the beginning/end of the aortic arch.

subtopic: Physiological features of the respiratory system
case_context: A healthy 22-year-old male is participating in a baseline respiratory assessment for a sports science study. He is asked to perform several breathing manoeuvres while connected to a spirometer.
additional_context: The participant is asked to perform a breath-hold, which triggers the body's homeostatic response to changing arterial blood gas levels.
question: Identify the two anatomical structures that house the peripheral chemoreceptors and name the cranial nerve that transmits sensory information from the receptors located in the neck to the medulla.
acceptable_answers: Carotid bodies and aortic bodies; Glossopharyngeal nerve
Carotid and aortic bodies; CN IX
Carotid body and aortic body; Glossopharyngeal
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the respiratory system] Peripheral chemoreceptors are located in the carotid bodies (at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries) and the aortic bodies (in the aortic arch). The carotid bodies signal via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), while the aortic bodies signal via the vagus nerve (CN X).

subtopic: Anatomical features of the gastrointestinal tract and liver, and abdomen
case_context: A 45-year-old male is undergoing an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During the procedure, the surgeon identifies the blood supply to the upper gastrointestinal organs and explains the normal anatomical relationships within the foregut.
question: Name the three main branches of the celiac trunk that provide the arterial supply to the stomach and other foregut structures.
feedback: [Subtopic: Anatomical features of the gastrointestinal tract and liver, and abdomen] The celiac trunk is the main artery of the foregut, arising from the abdominal aorta at the T12 level. It gives off the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries.

case_context: A 45-year-old male is undergoing an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During the procedure, the surgeon identifies the blood supply to the upper gastrointestinal organs and explains the normal anatomical relationships within the foregut.
additional_context: The surgical team discusses the normal secretory functions of the stomach mucosa that must be maintained for proper digestion.
question: Identify the specific cell type in the gastric glands responsible for secreting hydrochloric acid, and name ONE of the three primary neurohumoral molecules that directly stimulate these cells to produce acid.
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the gut] Parietal (oxyntic) cells produce HCl. Their acid secretion is stimulated by the binding of gastrin (to CCK2 receptors), histamine (to H2 receptors), and acetylcholine (to M3 receptors).

subtopic: Histology of the gastrointestinal tract and liver
case_context: A 45-year-old male is undergoing an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During the procedure, the surgeon identifies the blood supply to the upper gastrointestinal organs and explains the normal anatomical relationships within the foregut.
additional_context: The surgeon notes that the stomach is uniquely adapted for mechanical digestion.
question: The stomach wall contains an additional layer of smooth muscle in its muscularis externa compared to the rest of the GI tract. Name this specific layer.
feedback: [Subtopic: Histology of the gastrointestinal tract and liver] While most of the GI tract has two layers of muscularis externa (inner circular and outer longitudinal), the stomach has a third, innermost 'oblique' layer to facilitate the churning and mechanical breakdown of food.

subtopic: Embryonic development of the gastrointestinal tract and liver
case_context: A 45-year-old male is undergoing an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During the procedure, the surgeon identifies the blood supply to the upper gastrointestinal organs and explains the normal anatomical relationships within the foregut.
question: Name the embryological division from which the stomach originates and state the vertebral level at which the artery supplying this division typically arises from the abdominal aorta.
feedback: [Subtopic: Embryonic development of the gastrointestinal tract and liver] The stomach is a derivative of the embryonic foregut. The foregut is supplied by the celiac trunk, which originates from the aorta at the level of the T12 vertebra.

subtopic: Physiological features of the liver, gallbladder and pancreas
case_context: A 45-year-old male is undergoing an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During the procedure, the surgeon identifies the blood supply to the upper gastrointestinal organs and explains the normal anatomical relationships within the foregut.
additional_context: The surgeon reflects on how the exocrine pancreas normally responds to the arrival of acidic chyme in the duodenum.
question: State the primary inorganic ion secreted by the ductal cells of the exocrine pancreas and name the hormone that primarily stimulates its release in response to low duodenal pH.
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the liver, gallbladder and pancreas] Secretin is released from S-cells in the duodenum in response to acid. It stimulates pancreatic duct cells to secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid to neutralize the chyme.

case_context: A 68-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department after suddenly developing weakness in his right arm and leg, and difficulty speaking. A neurological examination identifies a deficit in the primary motor cortex of the left hemisphere.
question: In which specific gyrus of the cerebral cortex is the primary motor cortex located?
feedback: [Subtopic: Neuroanatomy] The primary motor cortex is located in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe, which is situated immediately anterior to the central sulcus.

case_context: A 68-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department after suddenly developing weakness in his right arm and leg, and difficulty speaking. A neurological examination identifies a deficit in the primary motor cortex of the left hemisphere.
additional_context: The patient's symptoms suggest a vascular event affecting the blood supply to the lateral aspect of the left cerebral hemisphere.
question: Name the specific cerebral artery that supplies the lateral aspect of the hemisphere AND the arterial circle located at the base of the brain from which the cerebral arteries originate.
acceptable_answers: Middle cerebral artery and Circle of Willis
Middle cerebral artery and circulus arteriosus cerebri
feedback: [Subtopic: Neuroanatomy] The middle cerebral artery (MCA) supplies the majority of the lateral surface of the brain. It originates from the Circle of Willis (circulus arteriosus cerebri), which provides collateral circulation at the base of the brain.

case_context: A 68-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department after suddenly developing weakness in his right arm and leg, and difficulty speaking. A neurological examination identifies a deficit in the primary motor cortex of the left hemisphere.
additional_context: Signals from the motor cortex are transmitted via action potentials along axons to the spinal cord.
question: During the depolarization phase of a normal action potential, state the specific ion that moves across the neuronal membrane AND the direction of its net movement (into or out of the cell).
feedback: [Subtopic: Neurophysiology] Depolarization is caused by the opening of voltage-gated sodium (Na+) channels, allowing a rapid influx of sodium ions into the cell down their electrochemical gradient.

case_context: A 68-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department after suddenly developing weakness in his right arm and leg, and difficulty speaking. A neurological examination identifies a deficit in the primary motor cortex of the left hemisphere.
additional_context: Efficient signal transmission in the central nervous system depends on the histological structure of the axons.
question: Name the specific glial cell responsible for the myelination of axons in the brain AND the term for the periodic gaps in this myelin sheath where ion exchange occurs.
feedback: [Subtopic: Neurohistology] In the central nervous system, oligodendrocytes produce the myelin sheath. The gaps between myelin segments are the Nodes of Ranvier, which facilitate saltatory conduction.

subtopic: Psychiatry and psychological & sociological principles in behavioural neuroscience
case_context: A 68-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department after suddenly developing weakness in his right arm and leg, and difficulty speaking. A neurological examination identifies a deficit in the primary motor cortex of the left hemisphere.
additional_context: While checking the patient's recovery, he reports that while he can feel the touch of a pen on his arm (sensation), he struggles to recognize the object without looking at it.
question: State the psychological term used to describe the mental process of organizing and interpreting sensory information to recognize objects or environments.
feedback: [Subtopic: Psychiatry and psychological & sociological principles in behavioural neuroscience] Sensation is the physical detection of stimuli, whereas perception is the higher-order psychological process of interpreting that sensory information.

case_context: A 68-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department after suddenly developing weakness in his right arm and leg, and difficulty speaking. A neurological examination identifies a deficit in the primary motor cortex of the left hemisphere.
additional_context: The motor signals travel through the corticospinal tract, which decussates before reaching the spinal cord nerves that innervate the limbs.
question: Name the specific part of the brainstem where the decussation of the pyramids (corticospinal tracts) occurs.
feedback: [Subtopic: Neuroanatomy] The decussation of the pyramids occurs in the lower (caudal) part of the medulla oblongata, explaining why the left hemisphere controls the right side of the body.

topic: F. Skin, UroGenital, Endocrine and Reproduction (SUGER)
subtopic: Physiological features of the renal and urinary system
case_context: A 28-year-old woman attends her first antenatal appointment at 12 weeks gestation. She is healthy with no significant past medical history. Routine blood tests are performed as part of her antenatal care. The GP notes her serum creatinine is 45 µmol/L (normal range for non-pregnant female: 45-90 µmol/L).
question: State the physiological change in Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) that occurs during normal pregnancy, which typically accounts for this lower serum creatinine concentration.
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the renal and urinary system] During normal pregnancy, renal plasma flow and GFR increase significantly (often by 50%). This leads to more efficient clearance of creatinine, resulting in lower baseline serum creatinine levels compared to the non-pregnant state.

topic: F. Skin, UroGenital, Endocrine and Reproduction (SUGER)
subtopic: Physiological features of the reproductive system
case_context: A 28-year-old woman attends her first antenatal appointment at 12 weeks gestation. She is healthy with no significant past medical history. Routine blood tests are performed as part of her antenatal care. The GP notes her serum creatinine is 45 µmol/L (normal range for non-pregnant female: 45-90 µmol/L).
additional_context: The patient is curious about the hormonal changes maintaining her pregnancy during this first trimester.
question: Name the specific ovarian structure that is the primary source of progesterone required to maintain the endometrium during the first 8-10 weeks of pregnancy.
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the reproductive system] The corpus luteum is formed from the remains of the ovarian follicle after ovulation. In early pregnancy, it is rescued from degeneration by human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) and continues to secrete progesterone until the placenta takes over steroidogenesis around week 10.

topic: F. Skin, UroGenital, Endocrine and Reproduction (SUGER)
subtopic: Physiological features of the endocrine system

additional_context: As the pregnancy progresses towards term, the maternal body prepares for labour and delivery.
question: Name the hormone secreted by the posterior pituitary gland that is responsible for stimulating uterine smooth muscle contractions during the second stage of labour.
feedback: [Subtopic: Physiological features of the endocrine system] Oxytocin is synthesized in the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary. During labour, stretching of the cervix triggers its release, which in turn stimulates uterine contractions in a positive feedback loop.

question: Name the specialized multinucleated outer layer of the placental trophoblast that is in direct contact with the maternal blood in the intervillous space.
feedback: [Subtopic: Histology of SUGER] The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer, syncytial layer of the trophoblast that actively invades the uterine wall. It lacks individual cell boundaries and forms the primary barrier and transport surface between maternal blood and fetal tissues.

question: State the term for the third and final stage of renal development that forms the definitive adult kidney in humans.
feedback: [Subtopic: Embryonic development of the urogenital and reproductive organs] Human kidney development occurs in three successive stages: the pronephros (rudimentary), the mesonephros (interim), and the metanephros, which becomes the permanent kidney and starts functioning around the 10th-12th week of gestation.

case_context: A 68-year-old male presents to his GP for a routine health review. He is concerned about his skeletal health and mentions he has increased his dietary intake of calcium and started daily walking to maintain his bone strength.
question: Name the two types of bone cells that must be 'coupled' to ensure balanced bone remodeling (1 mark) and identify which of these two cell types expresses the RANK-ligand (RANKL) (1 mark).
feedback: [Subtopic: Bone] Bone remodeling involves the coordinated action (coupling) of bone-resorbing osteoclasts and bone-forming osteoblasts. Osteoblasts (and osteocytes) produce RANKL, which binds to the RANK receptor on osteoclast precursors to stimulate their differentiation and activity.

case_context: A 68-year-old male presents to his GP for a routine health review. He is concerned about his skeletal health and mentions he has increased his dietary intake of calcium and started daily walking to maintain his bone strength.
additional_context: The patient's blood tests are normal: Serum calcium 2.35 mmol/L [2.20-2.60 mmol/L]; Serum phosphate 1.1 mmol/L [0.8-1.5 mmol/L].
question: Describe the direct effect of parathyroid hormone (PTH) on renal phosphate handling (1 mark) and name the active form of Vitamin D produced by the kidneys in response to PTH stimulation (1 mark).
acceptable_answers: Decreases phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule; 1,25(OH)2D
feedback: [Subtopic: Biochemistry/homeostasis] PTH decreases the reabsorption of phosphate in the renal proximal convoluted tubule (promoting phosphaturia). It also stimulates the 1-alpha-hydroxylase enzyme to convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D into its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol).

case_context: A 68-year-old male presents to his GP for a routine health review. He is concerned about his skeletal health and mentions he has increased his dietary intake of calcium and started daily walking to maintain his bone strength.
additional_context: The GP explains that the strength of the femur is due to its organized microscopic structure.
question: Name the structural unit of compact (cortical) bone, consisting of concentric lamellae (1 mark), and name the small spaces within the matrix where mature bone cells are located (1 mark).
feedback: [Subtopic: Histology] The functional and structural unit of compact bone is the osteon (or Haversian system). Osteocytes reside in small cavities within the mineralized matrix called lacunae.

case_context: A 68-year-old male presents to his GP for a routine health review. He is concerned about his skeletal health and mentions he has increased his dietary intake of calcium and started daily walking to maintain his bone strength.
additional_context: The patient asks why walking is specifically recommended for his bones compared to non-weight-bearing activities like swimming.
question: According to the 'Mechanostat' model, identify the mature bone cell that acts as the primary mechanosensor (1 mark) and state the term for the process where bone is added to a surface without prior resorption in response to high mechanical strain (1 mark).
feedback: [Subtopic: Exercise] Osteocytes, embedded within the bone matrix, sense mechanical strain through their dendritic processes. When strain exceeds a certain threshold (the modeling threshold), bone modeling occurs, which involves the addition of new bone to strengthen the structure.

case_context: A 68-year-old male presents to his GP for a routine health review. He is concerned about his skeletal health and mentions he has increased his dietary intake of calcium and started daily walking to maintain his bone strength.
additional_context: A discussion occurs regarding the biochemical composition of the bone matrix that allows it to resist different types of forces.
question: Name the specific type of collagen that makes up approximately 90% of the organic bone matrix (1 mark) and name the mineral crystal that provides bone with its compressive stiffness (1 mark).
feedback: [Subtopic: Intro] Bone is a composite material. The organic component is predominantly Type 1 collagen, providing tensile strength (toughness), while the inorganic component is primarily hydroxyapatite crystals, providing compressive strength (stiffness).

question: Name TWO classes of medication, other than opioids, that are specifically recognized for their potential to cause physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms.
feedback: [Subtopic: Drugs associated with dependence and withdrawal symptoms (linked to 'Osteoarthritis / Chronic pain - EYGP session 11)] In addition to opioids, benzodiazepines (used for anxiety/insomnia) and gabapentinoids (used for nerve pain) are associated with dependence and require careful management and tapering.

subtopic: Routes of drug administration and medicine formulations (linked to 'Ischaemic heart disease / Health inequalities' - EYGP session 3)
case_context: A 42-year-old man visits his GP surgery to discuss his treatment for chronic back pain. He has been using over-the-counter paracetamol but feels it is no longer sufficient to manage his symptoms.

question: In the context of drug delivery, define the term 'systemic administration'.
acceptable_answers: Administration where the drug enters the circulatory system to be distributed throughout the body
The drug enters the bloodstream and travels to the whole body
Delivery to the blood for distribution to all tissues
feedback: [Subtopic: Routes of drug administration and medicine formulations (linked to 'Ischaemic heart disease / Health inequalities' - EYGP session 3)] Systemic administration refers to any route where the drug enters the bloodstream, allowing it to act on multiple sites throughout the body, unlike local administration which acts only at the site of application.

subtopic: Non-pharmacological interventions (linked to 'Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) / Functional disorders' - EYGP session 5)
